passage: Tutor's note, week three. I'm Himani, and I've watched Mehak change how maths homework happens. Before, the phone lay beside the book and every session began with Mehak's own scolding for looking at it. Now the phone sits in the hall drawer during study time. A fixed block, six to seven, is written on the wall calendar. On the desk lies only the maths book, one pencil and a glass of water. On Monday, Mehak finished eight problems in the hour and said, “I didn't fight myself once.” I said little. The surroundings did most of the work, and the daily scolding stopped. Next step for me: leave things as they are and watch how the routine holds up.

qa.q: Where does the phone sit during study time?
qa.a: The phone sits in the hall drawer during study time.

qa.q: What did Mehak mean by “I didn't fight myself once”?
qa.a: Mehak felt relieved and calm: without the phone nearby there was no temptation to resist, and the daily self-scolding stopped.

qa.q: What three changes to the surroundings did Mehak make?
qa.a: Mehak put the phone in the hall drawer, wrote a fixed block from six to seven on the calendar and kept only the maths book, a pencil and water on the desk.

qa.q: How might Himani feel watching the routine work?
qa.a: Himani is probably pleased and quietly hopeful, and chooses to say little so the routine stays Mehak's own.

grounding: A wise student changes the surroundings, phone away, fixed block, only the needed book, instead of scolding daily.

passage: Wednesday evening. Something worked today, so I'm writing it down. Reena said last week, “Stop trying to be strong, just move the temptation.” So I did the boring version. At 5:30 the phone went into the hall drawer. On my desk, only the physics book, a notebook and a pencil. I set the little alarm for 6:30. At first my hand kept reaching for the pocket that wasn't there, twice, and I laughed at myself. But then I was through two whole chapters before I looked up, and I hadn't even had to argue with myself. Nothing heroic. Just a drawer. Tomorrow same time, same drawer. — Shankar

qa.q: What time did Shankar put the phone in the hall drawer?
qa.a: Shankar put the phone into the hall drawer at 5:30.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when the hand reached for the empty pocket?
qa.a: Shankar felt amused at the habit, laughing at the twice-reaching hand, and not upset.

qa.q: What worked better than trying to be strong?
qa.a: Moving the phone into another place and keeping only the physics book, notebook and pencil on the desk meant there was nothing to argue with.

qa.q: How might Reena feel hearing that the advice worked?
qa.a: Reena would probably feel pleased and a little proud, since Reena's advice to move the temptation, not be strong, made a difference.

grounding: A wise student puts the phone in another room, keeps a fixed block and only the needed book, rather than scolding themselves.

passage: In Jaya's village near Sirsi, the only good signal was on the roof, and the only quiet place was her grandmother's room. With board exams two months away, Jaya made a plan. Every evening from six to eight, she gave her phone to Ajji, who put it in the steel cupboard. On the small wooden desk she kept only that day's book and a pencil. Her cousin Yusuf laughed. "You'll go mad." For the first three days, she did. Her hand kept reaching for nothing. By the second week, she was finishing a full chapter each evening. She stopped scolding herself before bed, because there was nothing to scold.

qa.q: From what time to what time did Jaya give her phone away?
qa.a: From six to eight every evening.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel in the first three days?
qa.a: She felt restless and a little frustrated, her hand reaching for the missing phone.

qa.q: Which choice helped Jaya most?
qa.a: Giving the phone to Ajji and keeping only one book on the desk changed the surroundings, so she didn't have to fight herself every evening.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Jaya's plan after two weeks?
qa.a: Yusuf, who laughed at first, might be surprised and impressed that she was finishing a chapter each evening.

grounding: Shows a student using a fixed study block, a phone kept in another room and a clear desk instead of daily self-scolding.

passage: Mateo, sixteen, lived in a small flat in Buenos Aires with his sister Ada, who was studying for university entrance. Mateo was always behind; Ada never was. One night he asked her secret. She pointed at her desk: one textbook, one notebook, a glass of water. "Phone's in the kitchen drawer till nine. I start at seven, same time every day." "That's it?" "That's it. Before, I used to promise myself to be strong and then feel terrible." Mateo tried it the next evening, clearing his desk of comics and chargers. He felt twitchy for twenty minutes, then forgot the drawer. He finished his chemistry questions by half past eight.

qa.q: Where does Ada keep her phone during study time?
qa.a: Ada keeps it in the kitchen drawer till nine.

qa.q: How did Mateo feel during the first twenty minutes?
qa.a: He felt twitchy and restless without the phone, before forgetting about the drawer.

qa.q: What steps did Mateo copy from Ada?
qa.a: He cleared his desk of comics and chargers, kept the phone away and started at a fixed time, which let him finish by half past eight.

qa.q: How might Ada see her old way of promising to be strong?
qa.a: Ada sees it as a trap that left her feeling terrible, which is why she changed her surroundings instead.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning from a sibling to shape the study environment rather than rely on willpower.

passage:
Evening study time in the girls' hostel ran from seven to nine. Most girls studied on their beds, phones beside them.
Alka didn't. At 6:55 she walked to the warden's desk and put her phone in the small locker the hostel offered, which almost nobody used. Then she went to the study room, not her bed. She took only the chemistry book and one notebook. Her other books stayed in the room.
Her roommate Pallavi followed her the first week, curious. "Don't you get bored without your phone?"
"For the first ten minutes. Then I forget it exists."
"I just tell myself not to look."
"How's that going?"
Pallavi laughed. "I looked eleven times yesterday."
Alka shrugged. "I used to scold myself every night. It never worked. Moving the phone works."
By the second week, Pallavi's phone was in the locker next to Alka's. In the unit test, both of them did better than in the last one.

qa.q: Where did Alka put her phone?
qa.a: In the small locker the hostel offered, at the warden's desk.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel about Alka's routine at first?
qa.a: Pallavi was curious and a little doubtful, asking if Alka got bored without the phone.

qa.q: Why does Alka's method work better than scolding herself?
qa.a: Changing the surroundings removes the pull, with the phone in a locker, a fixed study room and only one book, so there is nothing to resist.

qa.q: How does Pallavi's view change by the second week?
qa.a: Pallavi comes to see that moving the phone works, and puts her own phone in the locker next to Alka's.

grounding: Illustrates a student who puts her phone away, uses a fixed study block and keeps only the needed book, shaping her surroundings instead of scolding herself.
